system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2173-09-12 00:35:00 to 2173-09-12 17:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with worsening pain at her G-tube site, persistent despite a recent tube exchange and prior steroid injection. Imaging showed inflammatory changes around the tube without abscess or infection. Pain was initially managed with oxycodone but transitioned to oral hydromorphone (dilaudid) with improved control. A trial of bolus tube feeds was unsuccessful due to hypoglycemia, so she was maintained on continuous feeds. The patient remained stable, afebrile, and hemodynamically normal throughout the stay. She was discharged home on continuous tube feeds (NutriHep at 50 cc/hr), dilaudid for breakthrough pain, and instructions to monitor blood glucose and follow up with her surgeon.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to ___ with 
pain at your G-tube site. You were given Oxycodone with good 
effect. Please resume your home continuous tube feeds (NutriHep 
@ 50 cc/hour). Continue to monitor your blood sugars when you 
return home.

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:

*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.

*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.

*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.

*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.

*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.

*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.

*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.

*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.

*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids.

Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.

Please follow up with your surgeon Dr. ___ at the 
appointment listed below.

Best wishes,
Your ___ surgical team

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team members. You're here because of increasing pain around your G-tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's been sharp and constant since this morning. I ran out of my oxycodone, and Tylenol isn’t helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you've had this pain before and were admitted a few times. The last CT showed inflammation, but no infection or abscess. We’ll keep you overnight for pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds familiar. Is it the same issue again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely yes. Your exam today shows no redness or swelling around the tube, and your vitals are stable. We’ll start you on oxycodone to see how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’m just worried it won’t help like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. If oral meds aren’t enough, we can use IV Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. For now, you’ll stay on continuous tube feeds—NutriHep at 50 cc/hr.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that at home. No issues with the feeds themselves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re not seeing signs of infection—no fever or lab abnormalities. We’ll continue watching your pain and response to medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain now after the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’d say it’s down from a 7 to about a 3. I’m glad the medicine’s working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep you on the same plan for now. You’re still on continuous tube feeds, and we’ll continue monitoring your intake and output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I keep checking my blood sugar like at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Given your history of hypoglycemia after gastric bypass, it’s important to monitor regularly. We’ll remind you before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just completed an enteral infusion to ensure your feeds are running smoothly. You’re doing well—no nausea or discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even notice. It feels normal, which is a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. Pain is controlled, you’re afebrile, and labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume your regular tube feeds at 50 cc/hr, continue monitoring blood sugar, and take oxycodone 10 mg every 4 hours as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain doesn’t get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your surgeon or return to the ED if pain worsens, doesn’t improve in a few hours, or if you develop fever, chills, or other new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up with my surgeon and take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, avoid driving or alcohol while on oxycodone. Keep taking your other regular medications like fluoxetine, atenolol, and rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember from last time. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. A nurse will give you written instructions and your prescription for oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate the help getting the pain under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for sharp pain at her G-tube site, which had worsened after running out of oxycodone. She had a history of similar episodes with prior admissions showing inflammatory changes without infection. On admission, she was started on oxycodone with good pain control and remained on continuous tube feeds (NutriHep at 50 cc/hr). She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable throughout. IV Dilaudid was available for breakthrough pain but not required after initial oral dosing. An enteral infusion was completed without issues. She was discharged home with a prescription for oxycodone, instructions to resume home feeds and monitor blood glucose, and advised to follow up with her surgeon.
